title: The Anahata chakra in the destiny matrix: what your three heart arcana say

seo.title: Anahata in the destiny matrix: its three arcana and what they mean
seo.description: Anahata in the destiny matrix: where it sits, how to find its three arcana in a minute, what each means, and a birth-year check that catches errors.

short: Anahata is the heart chakra, the fourth of seven. In the destiny matrix it is the fourth row of the chakra table, and its theme is closeness and mutual care: how you love, what keeps you beside a person and what you feel while you are there. The row holds three arcana. Physics shows what your love looks like in action. Energy shows what feeds your care and what makes it fade. Emotions show how closeness resonates inside you. The first two numbers come from the two points that stand nearest the centre of the chart; the third is their sum. Anahata takes arcana from 3 to 22: The Magician and The High Priestess never land here. There are 393 possible rows, and even the most common, 5 / 5 / 10, comes up on roughly one date in 145.

sections.h2: Anahata in the matrix: a heart right beside the centre of the chart
paragraphs: **Where it sits.** Take the two rays that run into the centre of the matrix: the left one starts from the arcanum of your birth day, the top one from your birth month. Each ray carries several points, and the last one before the centre belongs to Anahata: on the left ray it is point S (physics), on the top ray point T (energy). Nowhere on the chart is there a point closer to the centre. Anahata stands right up against the core of the matrix.

**What it is made of.** Point S is the sum of the inner left point and the centre; point T is the sum of the inner point of talent, the inner point at the top, and the centre. The inner points make up the Vishuddha row, and the centre is Manipura. So in the matrix Anahata is counted from its two neighbours: Manipura, the chakra of will, is added to Vishuddha, the chakra of the word. That is how the formula is built, not proof of anything, but the rhyme is exact: in this scheme, the way you love is put together from what you say and what you stand on.

**What it is about.** The Sanskrit word anahata is usually translated as “unstruck” or “unhurt”: in the yogic tradition it names the sound that rings by itself, without any blow. Anahata is the middle one of the seven chakras. The three below it are in charge of support, desire and will; the three above it, of the word, understanding and meaning. In the tarot tradition our readings draw on, the theme of the heart is wider than romance. Benebell Wen, the author of Holistic Tarot, writes that the heart chakra position in her spread “indicates love and relationships, though it might also speak more generally about the Seeker’s compassion for humanity, sense of charity and benevolence.” In essence, she says, this card shows **“how kind the Seeker is”**, and through that, how the person approaches love.

That is why Anahata in the matrix is not “the romance chakra”. It is your way of being close to anyone at all: a partner, your mother, a friend, a child, a colleague who is going through a bad patch. And it runs in two directions: the theme of the row is **mutual** care, that is, how you give warmth and how you take it in. Quite often one of the two comes easier than the other.

paragraphs.h3: Anahata, the relationship line and the “arcanum under the heart” are not the same thing

paragraphs: These three get mixed up all the time, although they are counted from different points and answer different questions.

head: Anahata
Relationship line M–R1–R
“Under the heart” (point R1)
rows: the fourth row of the chakra table
a line in the lower right part of the chart
the middle of the relationship line
how you love in general: care, need, feeling
the couple’s script: the way in, the main knot, everyday life and money
what becomes the couple’s main question once the first attraction has passed

paragraphs: If you came here looking for the “arcanum under the heart”, you need point R1, which has an article of its own. Anahata explains something else: why you care the way you do, with everyone and not only within a couple.

sections.h2: How to work out your Anahata from your date of birth in a minute
paragraphs: All you need is addition and one rule: **if a sum is greater than 22, add its digits** (23 → 5, 29 → 11, 40 → 4). Repeat until you get a number from 1 to 22.

ol: **B** is the number of the month.
**C** is the sum of the digits of the year: 1993 → 22, 1985 → 23 → 5.
**D** = A + B + C. **E** (the centre) = A + B + C + D.
Inner points: **J** = A + E, **K** = B + E. This is the Vishuddha row.
**Anahata’s physics** S = J + E. **Energy** T = K + E. **Emotions** = S + T.

paragraphs: Example: someone born on 4 March 1993.

The Anahata row is **12 / 11 / 5**. If you already have your chakra table, there is no need to start from scratch: add the centre (the Manipura number) to Vishuddha’s physics and energy. 8 + 4 = 12, 7 + 4 = 11, and you get the same row.
If you would rather not count by hand, the calculator builds the whole chakra table at once. The arcana are shown free of charge and with no sign-up.

paragraphs.h3: The birth-year check: the third number knows your year

paragraphs: Anahata has a property that almost nobody writes about. **Add up the digits of your year of birth, then add the third number of your Anahata: the result is a multiple of nine, that is 9, 18, 27, 36 or 45.**

ul: 15 July 1985: 1 + 9 + 8 + 5 = 23; Anahata for this date is 15 / 7 / 22, and 23 + 22 = **45**.

paragraphs: Why it works. Write the Anahata formula out in full and you will find that the day and the month each enter the emotions exactly nine times. Adding digits does not change the remainder after division by nine, so as the sums are reduced, the day and the month drop out and only the year is left. We tested the rule on all 46,021 dates from 1900 to 2025, and there are no exceptions.

Two practical conclusions follow. First, if the check does not add up, the calculation has a mistake in it, most often a missed reduction of a number above 22. Second, everyone born in the same year has one of just two or three possible third numbers in Anahata.

head: Year of birth
Anahata emotions
rows: 4 · The Emperor, 13 · Death or 22 · The Fool
3 · The Empress, 12 · The Hanged Man or 21 · The World
10 · The Wheel of Fortune or 19 · The Sun

paragraphs: The rows repeat every nine years: 1944 belongs with 1953, and 2026 with 2017. Where there are two options, the smaller number comes up in roughly three cases out of four. Which one you get is decided by your day and month. This is a property of the formula, not a “generational feeling”: the year narrows the choice to two or three cards, and the date does the rest.

paragraphs.h3: Anahata 9 / 7 / 16: what it means and how to check the sum

paragraphs: If your Anahata shows 9, 7 and 1, go back over the calculation. In the classic matrix The Magician (1) never lands in Anahata, in any column, and the third number is always the sum of the first two. 9 + 7 = 16, so the correct row is **9 / 7 / 16**: The Hermit in physics, The Chariot in energy, The Tower in emotions. The year check confirms it. This Anahata only occurs for people born in 1982, 1991, 2000, 2009 and 2018, and in the earlier years of the same series: 1973, 1964, 1955. Take 3 January 1982: 1 + 9 + 8 + 2 = 20, and 20 + 16 = 36.

How it reads. The Hermit in action: you first think things through on your own and come to the person you love with words already weighed. The Chariot in motive: you care where the relationship is heading, and you need a shared road and a next step. The Tower in feeling: if that road rested on things left unsaid, the discovery feels not like a crack but like a collapse. The strength of this row is forethought: it is easy to lean on someone who arrives not on impulse but with a plan. The weak spot is in the same place: a plan made alone is easily mistaken for a shared one. So the main check for 9 / 7 / 16 is to ask the other person what they think before the route is ready, not after.

sections.h2: How to read Anahata: three numbers, one picture
paragraphs: The reference below gives the meaning of every card in every column. But a row is not three separate labels. It is easier to read in four steps.

ol: **Write out the row with the column names.** The order matters: 12 / 11 / 5 and 11 / 12 / 5 are different rows, and both occur.
**Read each card in its own column:** physics is the action, energy the motive, emotions the feeling.
**Find one sentence that ties all three together.** Not “The Hanged Man plus Strength plus The Hierophant”, but a thought you can recognise in your own life.
**Look for the difficulty along the same lines.** A row’s weak spot is usually its strength pushed to the limit.

paragraphs: Here is how it works in practice. Below is Anahata 12 / 11 / 5 from the full reading, word for word.

**Riding out their storm, keeping the bond** 12 · The Hanged Man — pausing to see their side. 11 · Strength — holding strong feelings steady. 5 · The Hierophant — trust in shared promises. With you, someone close doesn’t have to keep up a brave face. Care in Anahata begins with The Hanged Man: you set your own affairs aside and look at what is happening through the other person’s eyes, in no hurry to hand over ready-made advice. Strength fuels this involvement: you want to stay close when feelings run high, without suppressing either the feelings or the person. Trust comes through The Hierophant — in a relationship that has a recognised shape: promises, traditions, your own “this is how we do things”. After a hard day, someone close to you snaps and says more than they mean. You don’t answer in kind, and you don’t rush to fix their mood. You listen until the storm dies down, even though you had other plans for the evening — and behind the sharpness you make out the exhaustion. The next morning, the usual breakfast together says without words: we’re still us. **Around you, strong feelings don’t break the bond — they have somewhere to settle.** One person easily drops out of this picture — you. Seeing through the other’s eyes comes so naturally that your own things keep being put off: plans can wait, hurt can wait, a request can wait too. You calm your own storms as carefully as anyone else’s — and the person close to you may not even know you’re struggling. What’s left is holding on to the form: “this is what people do in a good relationship”. But when it replaces a real conversation, care becomes a duty done by the rulebook: everything is done properly, yet there is less and less warmth.

Look at what has been done here. Strength is read not as force or self-assurance but as the ability to ride out someone else’s storm: not answering in kind, not rushing to fix their mood, but hearing them out. The Hanged Man is not patience but a readiness to drop your plans for the evening and see the exhaustion behind the sharpness. The Hierophant holds the bond together through form: the usual breakfast the next morning says without words that you are still you. The trap grew out of the same combination: in this kind of care it is easy to forget yourself, and the form starts to stand in for a real conversation. Change one card and the picture changes. Every one of the 393 rows in the reading is written this way.

sections.h2: The arcana in Anahata: what each number means in all three columns
paragraphs: Anahata takes 20 arcana, from The Empress (3) to The Fool (22). The most frequent card here is The Hierophant: it appears in the row in 22% of calculations. The rarest is The Hanged Man, at 9%. First a cheat sheet to help you find your cards quickly, then each card in detail.

head: Arcanum
Physics: how you love in practice
Energy: what keeps you close
Emotions: what you feel
rows: taking charge of how life is run
keeping your word and your customs
the joy of choosing each other
the lift of a shared stride
a firm word in a gentle voice
not acting in the heat of the moment
a feeling that needs a pause
letting go of the old image
the sadness and relief of change
a strong pull towards your person
helping a dream along with deeds
believing in the person you love
a fine response and anxious guesses
being openly glad of the person
the call of your own people, belonging
a whole where each stays themselves
trying things together for the first time

paragraphs: For each card below you will find its image in the theme of the heart, the three columns and the trap: what this strength turns into if it goes unnoticed. These are symbolic themes to recognise yourself in, not verdicts on your character.

paragraphs.h3: 3 · The Empress: love that feeds

paragraphs: In Waite, The Empress is “the fruitful mother of thousands”, “all that is symbolized by the visible house of man”. In Anahata this is care that makes everything around it grow and feel lived in.

ul: **Physics:** care you can touch: feeding, warming, making things cosy, bringing a blanket at the right moment. Your love shows in your home.
**Energy:** the wish to make things grow, to see the person you love flourish and what you share grow stronger: a home, a family, a joint venture.
**Emotions:** the warmth of plenty. Joy when care comes back to you and “we have everything we need”.
**Trap:** care nobody asked for. Feeding someone who isn’t hungry and taking offence when they leave food on the plate. One day “I do so much for you” gets said out loud, and care turns into a debt.

paragraphs.h3: 4 · The Emperor: love as a solid roof

paragraphs: Waite writes that this card and that of the Empress “do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied”. His Emperor is “executive and realization, the power of this world”. In Anahata this is love expressed through running things and keeping them safe.

ul: **Physics:** taking on the running of your shared life: plans, money, repairs, safety. Your “I love you” sounds like “I’ll take care of it” and is proved by what gets done.
**Energy:** a need for stability and clear boundaries. You want to stay where the ground is firm underfoot and it is clear who is responsible for what.
**Emotions:** calm that comes from predictability. Irritation when the order is changed without you.

**Trap:** safety quietly turns into control: where are you, how much did you spend, why isn’t this going to plan. Wen pictures the price of such rule as a parched kingdom: there is order, but less and less life in it.

paragraphs.h3: 5 · The Hierophant: love that rests on what you share

paragraphs: The most common card in Anahata. In Waite’s list of divinatory meanings The Hierophant stands for “marriage, alliance” and, “by another account, mercy and goodness”. This is love that rests on shared values, customs and a word that is never broken.

ul: **Physics:** taking the union seriously. Keeping your word and cherishing customs: anniversaries, Sunday phone calls, the family table.
**Energy:** leaning on shared values. You stay when it is clear what you both believe in and what you are together for.
**Emotions:** trust in a shared word. Disappointment when the other person lives by different rules of “a proper relationship”.

**Trap:** form instead of meaning. Waite warns that the pontiff may forget “the significance of this his symbolic state” and act “as if he contained within his proper measures all that his sign signifies”. In a relationship these are rituals still kept after real conversation has stopped, or a “this is how it’s done in our family” that matters more than a living person.

paragraphs.h3: 6 · The Lovers: love as a mutual choice

paragraphs: Waite calls this “in all simplicity the card of human love”: two people stand unveiled before each other, in a love not yet “contaminated by gross material desire”. Wen adds the theme of choice. In Anahata this is love in which two people choose each other openly and freely. The Lovers turn up in roughly one calculated row in five.

ul: **Physics:** choosing the person plainly: saying “I’m with you”, introducing them to your friends, answering honestly, not leaving the relationship hanging.
**Energy:** a drive towards mutuality. It matters that both of you choose, by consent and not out of duty or fear of being alone.
**Emotions:** the joy of choosing each other, the tenderness of two people with nothing to hide from each other.

**Trap:** checking every decision of your own against the other person’s reaction, or demanding that the choice be confirmed anew every day. Mutuality turns into an exam that can never be passed for good.

paragraphs.h3: 7 · The Chariot: love on the move

paragraphs: Waite’s Chariot is “above all things triumph in the mind”, a conquest on planes that are “manifest or external and not within himself”. In Anahata this is love that needs a shared road and visible progress.

ul: **Physics:** taking the initiative. Suggesting a move, dreaming up a trip, steering a shared plan.
**Energy:** the wish to move forward together. A relationship is alive as long as you can see where you are going and there is a next step.
**Emotions:** excitement and the lift of a shared stride, the joy of a shared win.

**Trap:** driving for two. Waite’s charioteer wins on the outside, and in a couple you can likewise win the argument and lose the closeness, or rush the relationship forward without asking whether the other person wants to go there, and at that pace.

paragraphs.h3: 8 · Justice: an honest agreement

paragraphs: For Waite, Justice is the moral principle “which deals unto every man according to his works”. But beside it he sets gifts of another order, which “we have them or have not”, and adds that “the law of Justice is not however involved by either alternative”. In Anahata this is love that needs clarity and equal respect. In the emotions column Justice is one of the two most common cards.

ul: **Physics:** honestly carrying your share: agreeing who does what, and doing what was agreed.
**Energy:** a need for mutual respect: taking both people into account, deciding so that it is fair to both.
**Emotions:** relief once everything has been said. Hurt when an expectation nobody voiced is broken.

**Trap:** bookkeeping in love: “that’s the second time I’ve given in”, “I put in more”. Agreements live by the law of Justice, but love, as we read it, is closer to the gifts in that same passage of Waite: it is not credited according to merit.

paragraphs.h3: 9 · The Hermit: quiet depth

paragraphs: Waite’s Hermit stands on a height holding up a lamp that is not wrapped in his mantle: “where I am, you also may be.” In Anahata this is love that speaks quietly and thinks before it takes a step. In the emotions column it is the most common card, level with Justice.

ul: **Physics:** being quietly there: listening, giving room, not crowding. Thinking it over alone before suggesting anything.
**Energy:** a need to make sense of the relationship on your own: time and space to understand what you feel.
**Emotions:** a deep, restrained feeling that does not show at once. It is there; it simply lives deep down.

**Trap:** the lamp under the cloak. You went off to think, and the person you love decided they had been rejected. The love is there, but the other cannot see it. One sentence uncovers the lamp: “I need a little quiet. It’s not about you.”

paragraphs.h3: 10 · The Wheel of Fortune: love in waves

paragraphs: Waite sees in the Wheel “the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe” and “the flux of human life”, and stresses its “essential idea of stability amidst movement”. In Anahata these are relationships that live through stages and turns.

ul: **Physics:** flexibly rearranging your shared life when life turns a corner: a move, a new job, the birth of a child.
**Energy:** an interest in new stages. The relationship holds as long as it keeps renewing itself.
**Emotions:** feelings in waves: a lift at the turns, a lull on the straight stretches.

**Trap:** mistaking a lull for the end. Or waiting for the right moment to raise a question that has been piling up, and the moment never comes. The axle the changes turn on is one you have to hold yourselves.

paragraphs.h3: 11 · Strength: strong feeling in gentle hands

paragraphs: On Waite’s card a woman closes the jaws of a lion that “is being led by a chain of flowers”. The chain of flowers, he explains, signifies, among many other things, “the sweet yoke and the light burden of Divine Law, when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”, and the card “has nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense”. In Anahata this is the ability to stay in touch when things run hot.

ul: **Physics:** a firm word in a gentle voice. Saying something unpleasant with care, hearing disagreement out without steamrolling it.
**Energy:** staying close under strain, neither running from a quarrel nor going on the attack.
**Emotions:** strong attachment and compassion that need no damping down. The feeling is big, and the hands are gentle.

**Trap:** being strong for two for too long. Bottling up, smoothing over, “keeping it together”, until the lion breaks the chain of flowers. And separately: the gentleness of Strength does not oblige you to put up with what is destroying you.

paragraphs.h3: 12 · The Hanged Man: seeing it from the other side

paragraphs: The rarest card in Anahata. Waite insists that the Hanged Man’s face expresses “deep entrancement, not suffering”: this is “life in suspension, but life and not death”. Readings of the card as martyrdom and duty he calls false. In Anahata this is the pause in which you have time to see the situation through the other person’s eyes.

ul: **Physics:** not acting in the heat of the moment. Stopping, holding back your own rush, letting the person reach the decision themselves.
**Energy:** the wish to understand how it all looks from their side, and to see beyond your own desire.
**Emotions:** a feeling that needs a pause. You feel deeply but not at once, sometimes together with the other person’s pain.
**Trap:** the pause turns into sacrifice. Waiting, enduring, putting yourself off “for the sake of peace” is no longer Waite’s Hanged Man but the very martyrdom he argued against.

paragraphs.h3: 13 · Death: renewal through endings

paragraphs: On Waite’s card the horseman “carries no visible weapon”, and his black banner bears the Mystic Rose, “which signifies life”. The card itself, for him, is “change, transformation and passage”. In Anahata this is the ability to end what has served its time in a relationship: habits, roles, rules. Not necessarily the relationship itself.

ul: **Physics:** closing what has outlived itself through action: changing routines, scrapping old rules, ending the habits of “the people you used to be”.
**Energy:** a readiness to let go of the old image of the person you love and meet the one they have become.
**Emotions:** sadness and relief together. The end of a stage is lived deeply: the children have grown up, the roles have changed, the past cannot be brought back.
**Trap:** clinging to a dead form out of fear of change, or, the other way round, cutting everything off when a single habit has run its course. The card does not predict break-ups.

paragraphs.h3: 14 · Temperance: joining two lives

paragraphs: Waite’s angel pours “the essences of life from chalice to chalice”, with one foot on the earth and one on the waters. The card, in Waite’s words, “tempers, combines and harmonises”. In her example about relationships, Wen ties it to “a greater need for cooperation and tempering of extreme emotions”. In Anahata this is closeness built in small steps and at a shared pace.

ul: **Physics:** drawing closer in small, steady steps, matching different paces, agreeing on little things.
**Energy:** joining two lives without cancelling either, finding a shared measure.
**Emotions:** an even warmth that does not cool even in an argument.

**Trap:** peace at any price. Muting what is unpleasant for the sake of seeming agreement, and accepting a compromise that erases a boundary that matters to you. Coming to terms does not require giving yourself up.

paragraphs.h3: 15 · The Devil: the pull that holds

paragraphs: In Waite, two figures are chained to the Devil “as if Adam and Eve after the Fall”: this is “the chain and fatality of the material life”. He also notes that the one exalted above them is not “to be their master for ever”. And the Devil’s raised hand is, in Waite, “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant”, the most common card in Anahata. In Anahata The Devil is a strong pull and attachment. It appears in the row in 12% of calculations.

ul: **Physics:** closeness you can touch: gifts, shared things and money, physical closeness. You bind your lives together firmly.
**Energy:** a strong pull towards your person, an attraction that holds.
**Emotions:** clinging attachment, passion side by side with the fear of loss.

**Trap:** losing the difference between “I want to be with you” and “I want you to be mine”. Jealousy, checking up, “I can’t live without you”. The number itself says nothing about dependence: it shows how strongly you attach, and what you do with that force is up to you.

paragraphs.h3: 16 · The Tower: an honest foundation

paragraphs: Waite reads the Tower as the rending of “a House of Falsehood” and recalls the psalm: “except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it.” In Anahata this is love that cannot stand falseness. The Tower appears in the row in 12% of calculations.

ul: **Physics:** naming plainly what doesn’t work. Talking about hard things out loud and revising rules that have outlived themselves.
**Energy:** a need for an honest foundation. Where something rests on an untruth, you feel uneasy.
**Emotions:** a sharp response to untruth. A lie that comes out feels not like a crack but like a collapse.
**Trap:** bringing everything down in the moment of the blow. The Tower destroys a house of lies, not every house. Before you decide for good, separate the checked fact from the guess.

paragraphs.h3: 17 · The Star: faith in the other

paragraphs: Waite gives the Star’s mottoes as “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. Her figure pours water on both land and sea, and her gift, in Waite, reaches those below “in the measure that they can receive her influx”. In Anahata this is generous tenderness and faith in the person you love.

ul: **Physics:** helping a dream along with deeds: finding a course, freeing up an evening, being the first to look at the work.
**Energy:** the inspiration of growing side by side. It matters to you to believe in the person and to watch them grow bigger.
**Emotions:** generous tenderness and hope.

**Trap:** loving an image instead of a person, so that the one you love has to live up to your dream of them. Or giving more than the other can take in. In Waite the measure is the capacity to receive, not the generosity of the giver.

paragraphs.h3: 18 · The Moon: sensitivity to half-tones

paragraphs: Waite’s Moon is a path walked when “there is only reflected light to guide it”, where the dog and the wolf are “the fears of the natural mind”. In Anahata this is a fine sense of atmosphere and subtext.

ul: **Physics:** gentleness with what is unclear. You notice that something is off and approach it softly.
**Energy:** sensitivity to mood, hearing what lies beneath the words.
**Emotions:** a fine response to the other person’s state, and anxious guesses when you are near them.

**Trap:** filling in the dark. A short reply turns into “they’ve gone cold”, and you are now reacting to your own version. The Moon’s observation is often right; it is the explanation that goes wrong. The check is simple: ask.

paragraphs.h3: 19 · The Sun: open warmth

paragraphs: Waite’s Sun is direct light, “the direct as the antithesis of the reflected light”, and that light is “typified by the heart of a child”. In Anahata this is love that is not hidden.

ul: **Physics:** being openly glad of the person: hugging them in front of everyone, praising them, celebrating together.
**Energy:** sharing warmth and living without things left unsaid.
**Emotions:** the joy of being accepted as you are.
**Trap:** shining in the hope of a reflection. If there was less attention than you hoped for, you dim or start chasing admiration. The Sun shines; it does not wait to be shone on.

paragraphs.h3: 20 · Judgement: a call from within

paragraphs: Waite’s Judgement is transformation in answer to a summons that “is heard and answered from within”. On the card a man, a woman and their child rise from their tombs, but Waite deliberately adds others: “there are more than three who are restored”, and a reading through the family alone falls short. In Anahata this is the renewal of familiar roles and a sense of belonging.

ul: **Physics:** changing what you inherited through action. Seeing family roles from the outside and rebuilding them: who decides, who does the caring, how you quarrel.
**Energy:** answering the call of your own people, a need to belong and for a living bond.
**Emotions:** moments of clarity, when you can see that a stage is over and the relationship has come back to life.
**Trap:** repeating your parents’ script without noticing, or waiting for years for the person you love to “wake up” and change on their own.

paragraphs.h3: 21 · The World: a whole where each stays themselves

paragraphs: For Waite the World is fullness and completion, “the rapture of the universe when it understands itself in God”. In Anahata this is love with enough room for two different worlds.

ul: **Physics:** living broadly as two: joining your shared life with friends, work and separate interests.
**Energy:** seeing the union as a whole and accepting differences.
**Emotions:** a sense of a whole in which each of you stays yourself.
**Trap:** the picture of a harmonious couple becomes more important than an awkward conversation. A particular difficulty gets talked around with general words about how good everything is overall.

paragraphs.h3: 22 · The Fool: lightness and room to breathe

paragraphs: In the matrix 22 is The Fool; in Waite his number is 0. He is “the spirit in search of experience”, and for him “the edge which opens on the depth has no terror”. In Anahata this is love that needs air, play and novelty.

ul: **Physics:** trying things together for the first time: surprising each other, fooling around, turning off the familiar route.
**Energy:** room and lively interest. You want to be close as long as the relationship has air in it.
**Emotions:** carefree, almost childlike joy.
**Trap:** any commitment feels like a cage. Instead of the words “I need space”, a sudden disappearance. And the beginning delights more than what follows.

paragraphs: The reference answers the question “what does my card mean”. The question “what do my three cards mean together” is answered by the reading of the row, which is covered below.

sections.h2: Doubles, mirrors and rarities: Anahata by the numbers
paragraphs: We calculated Anahata for every date from 1 January 1900 to 31 December 2025, 46,021 dates in all. Here is what they show.

**One card in two columns.** Physics and energy match in 6.7% of calculations: 5 / 5 / 10, 9 / 9 / 18, 17 / 17 / 7 and so on, and a double is possible for each of the 20 arcana. A repeat does not mean “double strength”. One card shows itself in two roles, in action and in motive. In the row 5 / 5 / 10, The Hierophant in physics is loyalty to customs, and in energy it is reliance on shared views. A match is only possible when the day and the month of birth leave the same remainder after division by nine, as for people born on 3, 12, 21 or 30 March. But even for them it does not always happen.

**The Moon as a mirror.** When The Moon stands in physics or energy (this happens in 11% of calculations), in four cases out of ten the emotions repeat the other card: 18 / 6 / 6, 7 / 18 / 7, 18 / 9 / 9. The reason is arithmetic: add 18 to a number from 5 to 11, reduce the sum, and you get the same number back. But the rhyme with the card is exact. Waite’s Moon is reflected light, and in these rows the feeling reflects the neighbouring card. Read such a row this way: the feeling grows out of the other card, and The Moon adds a half-tone to it, a sensitivity and a habit of filling in the gaps.

**The most common and the rarest.** The most common Anahata is 5 / 5 / 10: 318 dates out of 46,021, roughly one date in 145. The rarest are 4 / 12 / 16 and 12 / 4 / 16. Each turned up only twice in 126 years, and all four dates fall in 2000: 4 and 31 March, 3 and 30 April.

**The “scary” cards.** Death, The Devil or The Tower stand in almost every third calculated Anahata, 31.6% of dates. Add The Moon and the figure reaches 43%. This is no verdict on your relationships: in the theme of the heart, each of these cards has a working side, whether honesty, the ability to end what has outlived itself, the strength of attachment or sensitivity.

**Which numbers never appear.** The Magician (1) and The High Priestess (2) never land in Anahata: both of its points come from addition, the small sums here are always greater than two, and the large ones reduce to between 3 and 12. In the emotions column small numbers come up more often: 11 or lower in 69% of calculations, while each number from 13 to 21 accounts for only 2–3%.
**The order of the columns matters.** 12 / 11 / 5 and 11 / 12 / 5 are different rows: in the first The Hanged Man stands in action, in the second in motive.

sections.h2: A “closed” Anahata, Anahata “in the minus” and other myths
paragraphs: **“My Anahata is closed, empty, weak.”** The row cannot tell you that. The numbers in the table are card numbers, not scores for how full something is: 22 is not “stronger” than 3, and The Sun is not “better” than The Tower. In the classic calculation all seven rows are always filled; there is no such thing as an empty chakra.

**“Anahata in the minus.”** “Plus” and “minus” are best understood as two ways of living the same row, not as a property of the person. The Hermit in emotions in the plus is a deep, quiet feeling. In the minus it is a feeling the person you love knows nothing about. The card is the same; the difference is whether the other person can see it.

**“Bad numbers.”** Death in Anahata does not predict a break-up, The Devil does not predict betrayal, and The Tower does not predict disaster. Each number describes how you love, not what will happen to you.

**“Anahata is the heart as an organ.”** No. The matrix says nothing about the body, and no number in this row describes how you feel physically. If something is troubling you physically, that is a question for a specialist, not for the matrix.
**“Anahata has to be opened or worked through.”** The numbers do not change. What changes is how you live your row. Three questions are enough to begin with, one for each column:

ul: **physics:** does my care give the person I love what they need, or what I know how to give?
**energy:** do I say out loud what I need in order to stay close?
**emotions:** does the person I love know what I feel, or do I just assume it is obvious anyway?

sections.h2: What you will find in the full reading
paragraphs: The reference above describes each card on its own. The interesting part begins when the three cards are read together: the same Strength sounds different next to The Hanged Man and next to The Fool. That is why the full reading is not stitched together from the reference. Each of the 393 possible Anahata rows has a text of its own.

paragraphs.h3: What it contains

ul: **a heading:** the main idea of your row;
**three captions:** what each card does in your particular combination;
**three paragraphs:** the theme and what each card brings, a whole picture with an example from life, and the trap that grows out of the same strength.

paragraphs: All seven chakras are read the same way: support (Muladhara), desire and pleasure (Svadhisthana), will and independence (Manipura), closeness (Anahata), speech and influence (Vishuddha), perception and understanding (Ajna), meaning and direction (Sahasrara). After the calculation the “Chakras and your arcana” table appears straight away and free of charge, with all 21 arcana and their names. Until the reading is unlocked, the rows show a padlock: the interpretations open together with the full reading.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation:** the classic destiny matrix of Natalia Ladini with points A–T: S = J + E, T = K + E, where J = A + E and K = B + E; emotions are S + T; every sum greater than 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The statistics cover all 46,021 dates from 1900 to 2025. The rule “year plus emotions is a multiple of nine” is derived from the formula and checked on every date.

**Card meanings:** A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922), and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the authors’ original wording. The theme of the heart chakra follows Wen’s seven chakras spread (chapter 14).

**Readings by column, traps and the texts for each combination:** the author’s interpretation. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix or divided a chakra into physics, energy and emotions.
The destiny matrix is an esoteric model for self-observation with no scientific evidence behind it. It is not a forecast and not advice on well-being, money or relationships.

intro: Below: how to work out your row by hand, how to check the calculation against your year of birth in ten seconds, what each arcanum means in each column, and how three cards add up to one picture.

faq.q: How do I find my Anahata from my date of birth?
faq.a: Work out points S and T with the formula above, or build the matrix in the calculator: Anahata is row 04 in the chakra table. Then check the result against your year: the sum of the year’s digits plus the third Anahata number must be divisible by nine.

faq.q: What does it mean if my Anahata has two identical numbers?
faq.a: One card stands in two roles, in action and in motive, and is read separately in each. It is neither a doubling of the quality nor an imbalance. This happens in 6.7% of calculations for dates from 1900 to 2025.

faq.q: Which arcana are bad in Anahata?
faq.a: None. Death, The Devil, The Tower and The Moon look frightening, but in the theme of the heart they describe the ability to end what has outlived itself, the strength of attachment, the need for honesty, and sensitivity. At least one of these cards appears in 43% of Anahata calculations for dates from 1900 to 2025.

faq.q: Why does another calculator give me different numbers?
faq.a: Usually for one of three reasons. The calculator uses a different scheme: here it is the classic matrix of Natalia Ladini with points A–T. The columns come in a different order. Or a reduction of a number above 22 was missed, and the year check catches exactly that mistake. “Chakra analysis by date of birth” is a separate method, not the destiny matrix, and its numbers will not match these.

faq.q: Are Anahata and the “arcanum under the heart” the same thing?
faq.a: No. “Under the heart” is the name for the partner point R1, the middle of the relationship line. Anahata is the chakra row about how you love and care for everyone close to you, not only within a couple.

faq.q: Is Anahata different for men and women?
faq.a: No. Gender plays no part in the calculation and changes neither the numbers nor what they mean.

The destiny matrix uses the old Marseille numbering, in which 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength. In Waite and in many tarot books these two cards swap places. The meaning rests on the card’s name, so when you compare with a reading from another guide, match it by name, not by number.
